title: Bonding and Molecular Structure
description: How atoms bond, what shapes molecules take, how orbitals describe bonds, and the forces between molecules.
overview: Properties that matter to a chemist, such as whether a substance is a gas or a solid, dissolves in water, conducts electricity or reacts with oxygen, follow from how its atoms are bonded and how its molecules are shaped. The same electrons and nuclei, arranged differently, give diamond or graphite, ethanol or dimethyl ether.

This chapter treats bonding at three levels. Lewis structures and VSEPR give a fast, qualitative picture of connectivity and shape. Valence bond theory and molecular orbital theory give the quantum mechanical picture. The last sections look at the weaker forces between molecules and the bonding in metals and ionic solids.
objectives: Classify a bond as ionic, polar covalent or nonpolar covalent from electronegativity.
Draw Lewis structures with formal charges and resonance, including exceptions to the octet rule.
Predict molecular geometry and polarity with VSEPR.
Assign hybridization and describe σ and π bonds.
Build molecular orbital diagrams for diatomic molecules and find bond order and magnetism.
Rank intermolecular forces and relate them to physical properties.
Explain metallic bonding and trends in lattice energy.

sections.title: Types of chemical bonds
body: A **chemical bond** is an attraction that holds atoms together because the combined system has lower energy than the separate atoms. Bonds are usually grouped into three types, though real bonds lie on a continuum between them.

list: An **ionic bond** is the electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion. It forms when one atom transfers electrons to another, typically between a metal and a nonmetal with a large electronegativity difference (ΔEN > about 1.7). Ionic compounds, often called **salts**, are brittle crystalline solids with high melting points.
A **covalent bond** is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, typically two nonmetals. A single bond shares one pair, a double bond two, a triple bond three.
In **metallic bonding**, valence electrons are delocalized over a lattice of cations (see the last section).

body: If the atoms in a covalent bond have different electronegativities, the shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom, and the bond is **polar**. The bond in H₂ (ΔEN = 0) is nonpolar, the bond in HCl (ΔEN = 0.96) is polar covalent, and the bond in NaCl (ΔEN = 2.23) is mostly ionic.

Bond length is the distance between nuclei at minimum energy, and bond energy is the energy to break one mole of the bond in the gas phase. For a given pair of atoms, more shared electron pairs (a higher **bond order**) give a shorter, stronger bond.

check.q: A bond between atoms with ΔEN ≈ 0.4 is best described as…
Compared with a C–C single bond, a C=C double bond is…

sections.title: Lewis structures
body: A **Lewis structure** shows valence electrons as bonds (lines) and **lone pairs** (dots). Most main-group atoms are stable with eight valence electrons, the **octet rule**, and hydrogen with two.

list: Count the total valence electrons. Add one per unit of negative charge; subtract one per unit of positive charge.
Draw a skeleton: the least electronegative atom (not H) in the center, with single bonds to the others.
Complete the octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs, then put any remaining electrons on the central atom.
If the central atom lacks an octet, convert lone pairs from outer atoms into double or triple bonds.

body: The **formal charge** of an atom assigns the electrons in each bond equally to its two atoms:

Of several valid structures, prefer the one with formal charges closest to zero, with negative charge on the more electronegative atom. When more than one structure with equal energy can be written, none is correct alone. The real molecule is a **resonance** hybrid, with electrons delocalized over all the structures. The structures differ only in electron placement, never in atom positions.

example.title: Nitrate ion
example.problem: Draw the Lewis structure of NO₃⁻.
solution: Valence electrons: 5 + 3(6) + 1 = 24. Place N in the center with three single bonds to O (6 electrons) and complete the octets of the O atoms (18 electrons). N has only six electrons, so convert one O lone pair into an N=O double bond.

That structure has formal charges N +1, double-bonded O 0 and each single-bonded O −1. It can be written in three equivalent ways, so the real ion has three identical N–O bonds of bond order 4/3, and each O carries −2/3 of the charge.

list: **Incomplete octets**: B and Be compounds, for example BF₃ (six electrons on B), which makes them strong Lewis acids.
**Odd-electron species** (radicals): NO (11 valence electrons) and NO₂ have an unpaired electron.

**Expanded octets**: atoms of period 3 and beyond, such as in SF₆ (12 electrons on S) and PCl₅. Modern calculations show that d orbitals contribute little. These **hypervalent** molecules are better described by delocalized multicenter bonding, but the expanded-octet Lewis structure remains a useful bookkeeping device.

check.q: How many valence electrons must appear in the Lewis structure of SO₄²⁻?
What is the formal charge on N in NH₄⁺?
Which species violates the octet rule by having an odd number of electrons?
check.why: BF₃ and SF₆ have an incomplete and an expanded octet, but an even number of electrons.

sections.title: Molecular shape: VSEPR
body: The valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (**VSEPR**) model says that **electron domains** around a central atom (each bond, whether single, double or triple, counts as one domain, as does each lone pair) arrange themselves as far apart as possible. The arrangement of domains is the electron-domain geometry. The **molecular geometry** names only the positions of the atoms.

Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, so repulsion follows the order lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond. This compresses bond angles: CH₄ (109.5°), NH₃ (107°) and H₂O (104.5°) all have four domains.

body.tip: In a trigonal bipyramid, lone pairs go in the equatorial positions, where they have fewer close neighbors at 90°. In an octahedron with two lone pairs, they sit opposite each other.

example.title: Predicting a shape
example.problem: Predict the shape of SF₄ and the approximate bond angles.
solution: S has 6 valence electrons, and four F atoms add four bonds. S has four bonding domains and one lone pair, five domains in all: trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.
The lone pair goes in an equatorial position, giving a **seesaw** molecular shape, with axial F–S–F about 173° and equatorial F–S–F about 102°, both compressed from the ideal 180° and 120°.

check.q: What is the molecular shape of XeF₄?
check.why: Xe has 4 bonds and 2 lone pairs, six domains in an octahedron, with the lone pairs opposite each other.

check.q: Why is the H–O–H angle in water (104.5°) smaller than the tetrahedral angle?
check.a: The two lone pairs repel the bonding pairs more strongly
wrong: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen
The hydrogen atoms repel each other

sections.title: Bond and molecular polarity
body: A polar bond has a **dipole**: partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻ separated by a distance. Each bond dipole is a vector pointing toward the more electronegative atom. Whether a molecule is polar depends on the vector sum of its bond dipoles, which depends on shape.
The **dipole moment** is μ = Q·r, measured in debyes (D; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). Gas-phase values: HCl 1.08 D, NH₃ 1.47 D, H₂O 1.85 D.

list: CO₂ and CCl₄ have polar bonds, but their symmetrical shapes (linear and tetrahedral) make the dipoles cancel, so the molecules are **nonpolar**.
H₂O (bent) and NH₃ (pyramidal) are polar, because the dipoles do not cancel.
CHCl₃ is polar because the C–H and C–Cl dipoles differ, while CCl₄ is nonpolar. BF₃ is nonpolar and NF₃ is polar, though both have three polar bonds, because one is planar and the other pyramidal.

body: Polarity determines solubility (“like dissolves like”), boiling point and how a molecule interacts with electric fields, including the microwaves in an oven.

check.q: Which molecule is nonpolar despite having polar bonds?

sections.title: Valence bond theory and hybridization
body: In **valence bond theory** a covalent bond forms when atomic orbitals overlap and share a pair of electrons. Overlap along the internuclear axis gives a **σ bond**. Sideways overlap of p orbitals, above and below the axis, gives a **π bond**. A single bond is one σ bond. A double bond is a σ and a π bond, and a triple bond is a σ and two π bonds.

Simple overlap of pure s and p orbitals cannot explain the 109.5° angles in methane, because carbon’s 2p orbitals are 90° apart. Pauling’s resolution is **hybridization**: atomic orbitals on the same atom mix to form equivalent **hybrid orbitals** pointing in the directions VSEPR predicts. The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed.

head: Electron domains
Hybridization
Geometry
Unhybridized p orbitals
Example
rows: C in CH₄, N in NH₃, O in H₂O
table.caption: Hybridization is assigned from the number of electron domains.

list: In ethane, each C is sp³, and the C–C bond is a σ bond that is free to rotate.

In ethene, each C is sp². Two of its three σ bonds go to H and one to the other C. The remaining 2p orbitals overlap sideways to form a π bond, which holds the six atoms in a plane and prevents rotation about the double bond.
In ethyne, each C is sp: a σ framework along a line, with two perpendicular π bonds.

body.note: Hybridization is a bookkeeping model, not a physical process. Its limitation is that it describes localized bonds, so it cannot explain delocalized bonding, as in benzene, or magnetism, as in O₂. Molecular orbital theory handles these.

check.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CO₂?
check.why: Carbon has two electron domains (two double bonds).

check.q: How many σ and π bonds are in HC≡C–CH=CH₂ (1-buten-3-yne)?
check.why: There are 3 C–C connections and 4 C–H bonds, so 7 σ bonds. The triple bond adds two π bonds and the double bond adds one.

sections.title: Molecular orbital theory
body: **Molecular orbital (MO) theory** treats electrons as occupying orbitals that extend over the whole molecule. The orbitals are built as linear combinations of atomic orbitals (LCAO). N atomic orbitals combine to give N molecular orbitals.

When two atomic orbitals combine in phase, they form a **bonding orbital**, lower in energy, with electron density concentrated between the nuclei. Combined out of phase, they form an **antibonding orbital**, higher in energy and with a node between the nuclei (marked with an asterisk). Electrons fill MOs from the bottom up, following the Pauli and Hund rules, as they fill atomic orbitals.

body.eq: bond order = ½ (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)

body.caption: The two 1s orbitals of H₂ combine into a bonding σ₁ₛ orbital, which holds both electrons, and an empty antibonding σ*₁ₛ orbital.

body: Helium shows why antibonding matters. In He₂ both σ₁ₛ and σ*₁ₛ would be full, giving bond order 0: no bond forms.

The 2s orbitals form σ₂ₛ and σ*₂ₛ. The 2p orbitals form a σ₂ₚ (head-on overlap) and two degenerate π₂ₚ orbitals (sideways overlap), with their antibonding counterparts. For B₂, C₂ and N₂, mixing between 2s and 2p makes π₂ₚ lower in energy than σ₂ₚ. For O₂ and F₂, 2s and 2p are far enough apart that σ₂ₚ lies below π₂ₚ.

body.key: MO theory predicts that O₂ has two unpaired electrons in its degenerate π*₂ₚ orbitals, so it is paramagnetic. Liquid oxygen is drawn into a magnet. Lewis structures and valence bond theory, which pair every electron, cannot explain this.

example.title: Bond order of oxygen species
example.problem: Compare the bond order and bond length of O₂⁺, O₂, O₂⁻ and O₂²⁻.
solution: O₂ has 8 bonding and 4 antibonding valence electrons: bond order (8 − 4)/2 = 2. Removing an electron from π*₂ₚ gives O₂⁺ with 3 antibonding electrons: (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5. Adding electrons to π*₂ₚ gives O₂⁻, the superoxide ion, with 5 antibonding electrons: 1.5, and O₂²⁻, the peroxide ion, with 6: 1.
Bond lengths follow the reverse order: O₂⁺ 112 pm, O₂ 121 pm, O₂⁻ 133 pm, O₂²⁻ 149 pm.

body: MO theory also explains delocalization. In benzene the six carbon p orbitals combine into six π MOs; the three bonding MOs hold six electrons spread over the entire ring. The **HOMO** (highest occupied MO) and **LUMO** (lowest unoccupied MO) of a molecule control much of its reactivity and its absorption of light.

check.q: What is the bond order of N₂?

sections.title: Intermolecular forces
body: Bonds hold atoms together within a molecule. **Intermolecular forces** act between molecules and are 10 to 100 times weaker, but they decide boiling points, melting points, viscosity, surface tension and solubility.

list: **London dispersion forces** act between all molecules. A momentary uneven distribution of electrons creates a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbor. Strength grows with the number of electrons and with **polarizability**, the ease of distorting the electron cloud, so large molecules attract more strongly. Dispersion explains why noble gases condense, and why boiling points climb with molar mass: CH₄ −162 °C, C₂H₆ −89 °C, C₈H₁₈ 126 °C.
**Dipole–dipole forces** act between polar molecules, which align with opposite partial charges close together. For molecules of similar size, polar ones boil higher.
**Hydrogen bonding** is a strong dipole–dipole interaction between an H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F in another molecule (or the same one). The attraction is 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹.
**Ion–dipole forces** act between an ion and a polar molecule and drive dissolution of salts in water, with strength 40–600 kJ mol⁻¹.

body: Hydrogen bonding is why water is a liquid at room temperature, why ice floats (the open hydrogen-bonded lattice is less dense than the liquid), and why DNA strands pair. In water each molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds.

example.title: Ranking boiling points
example.problem: Rank in order of increasing boiling point: CH₃CH₂CH₃, CH₃OCH₃, CH₃CH₂OH.
example.solution: All three have about 44–46 g mol⁻¹, so dispersion forces are similar. Propane is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces (−42 °C). Dimethyl ether is polar (−24 °C). Ethanol has an O–H group and forms hydrogen bonds (78 °C).

check.q: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
Why does the boiling point of the noble gases rise from He to Xe?
check.a: Larger atoms are more polarizable, so dispersion forces are stronger
wrong: Larger atoms form covalent bonds with each other

sections.title: Metallic and ionic solids
body: In **metallic bonding** the valence electrons are not tied to any one atom. They form a delocalized “sea” that holds the metal cations together. This explains why metals conduct electricity and heat (electrons move freely), are malleable and ductile (layers slide without breaking bonds), and are lustrous. In MO terms, N atomic orbitals give N closely spaced MOs that merge into a continuous band. An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with other elements: brass is Cu and Zn; steel is Fe with up to about 2% C, where the carbon atoms block the layers from slipping and make the metal harder.
An ionic crystal is held together by Coulomb attraction. The force between charges Q₁ and Q₂ a distance r apart is F ∝ Q₁Q₂/r², and the potential energy is

The **lattice energy** is the energy released when gaseous ions assemble into one mole of the solid, or equivalently the energy to separate it into gaseous ions. It rises with the ionic charges and falls as the ions get larger and farther apart.

head: Compound
Ion charges
Lattice energy (kJ mol⁻¹)
table.caption: Lattice energies. Doubling both charges roughly quadruples the energy.

body: Lattice energy cannot be measured directly. It is found from the **Born–Haber cycle**, an application of Hess’s law that adds up sublimation, ionization, bond dissociation, electron affinity and the measured enthalpy of formation. High lattice energy explains the high melting point of MgO (2852 °C) compared with NaCl (801 °C), and why ionic solids are hard but brittle: a shift of one layer brings like charges together.

check.q: Which has the larger lattice energy: MgO or NaCl?
check.why: The ion charges are +2/−2 instead of +1/−1, and the ions are smaller.

check.q: Why can metals be hammered into sheets without shattering?
check.a: Delocalized electrons keep bonding as layers slide past each other
wrong: The cations are held in fixed positions by covalent bonds
Metal bonds break and re-form as hydrogen bonds

quiz.q: Pauling electronegativities are H 2.20, C 2.55, O 3.44, F 3.98. Which bond is the most polar yet still classified as covalent (ΔEN below about 1.7)?
quiz.why: ΔEN is 1.43 for C–F, 1.24 for O–H, 0.89 for C–O and 0.35 for C–H. A difference above about 1.7 would be mostly ionic.

quiz.q: In ozone, written O=O–O with one lone pair on the central oxygen, what is the formal charge of the central O?
quiz.why: FC = 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1. The terminal single-bonded O has FC = 6 − 6 − ½(2) = −1.

quiz.q: Ozone has two equivalent resonance structures, O=O–O and O–O=O. What is the O–O bond order in the real molecule?
quiz.why: The resonance hybrid averages the structures: each bond is single in one and double in the other, so (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5. The value 4/3 belongs to species with three equivalent structures, such as nitrate.

quiz.q: Which molecule has an expanded octet on its central atom?
quiz.why: Cl in ClF₃ has three bonding pairs and two lone pairs, ten electrons in all. BeCl₂ has an incomplete octet, NO₂ has an odd number of electrons, and CH₄ obeys the octet rule.

quiz.q: What is the molecular shape of the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻?
quiz.why: S has 6 + 18 + 2 = 26 valence electrons: three bonds and one lone pair, four domains. Only the atoms count in the molecular shape, so it is pyramidal like NH₃.

quiz.q: What are the electron-domain geometry and the molecular shape of XeF₂?
quiz.why: Xe has two bonds and three lone pairs, five domains. The lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, so the two F atoms lie on the axis, 180° apart.

quiz.q: The H–N–H angle in NH₃ is 107°, between CH₄ (109.5°) and H₂O (104.5°). Why?
quiz.a: NH₃ has one lone pair, which compresses the bond angles less than the two in water
wrong: Nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen, which opens the angle
NH₃ has a double bond that pushes the hydrogens apart
Nitrogen atoms are larger than oxygen atoms
quiz.why: All three have four electron domains. A lone pair takes up more space than a bonding pair, so more lone pairs mean smaller bond angles.

quiz.q: Which of these molecules is polar?
quiz.why: SF₄ is seesaw shaped, so its bond dipoles do not cancel. SF₆ (octahedral), XeF₄ (square planar) and CS₂ (linear) are symmetric and nonpolar.

quiz.q: A diatomic molecule has partial charges of +0.200e and −0.200e separated by 130 pm. What is its dipole moment? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m)
quiz.why: μ = Qr = (0.200 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1.30 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 4.17 × 10⁻³⁰ C m, which is 1.25 D. Using the full electron charge instead of 0.200e gives 6.24 D.

quiz.q: What are the hybridizations of the two carbon atoms in acetonitrile, CH₃–C≡N?
quiz.a: The CH₃ carbon is sp³ and the nitrile carbon is sp
wrong: The CH₃ carbon is sp² and the nitrile carbon is sp
The CH₃ carbon is sp³ and the nitrile carbon is sp²
quiz.why: The CH₃ carbon has four σ bonds (four domains). The nitrile carbon has one σ bond to C and one to N (two domains) plus two π bonds, which use its two unhybridized p orbitals.

quiz.q: Rotation is easy about the C–C bond in ethane but not about the C=C bond in ethene. Why?
quiz.a: Twisting the double bond would break the sideways overlap of the p orbitals that forms the π bond
wrong: The σ bond in ethene is shorter, so the carbon atoms cannot move
Ethene carbons are sp hybridized, which locks the geometry
The hydrogens on ethene repel each other too strongly
quiz.why: The σ bond is symmetric about the bond axis and survives rotation. The π bond has its overlap above and below the axis, which depends on the p orbitals staying parallel.

quiz.q: What is the bond order of C₂²⁻?
quiz.why: C₂²⁻ has 8 + 2 = 10 valence electrons, the same as N₂: 8 bonding and 2 antibonding, so (8 − 2)/2 = 3. Neutral C₂ has bond order 2.

quiz.q: N₂ loses an electron to form N₂⁺. The N–N bond becomes
quiz.a: weaker and longer, because a bonding electron is removed
wrong: stronger and shorter, because the ion carries a positive charge
weaker and longer, because an antibonding electron is removed
unchanged, because the electron is lost from a nonbonding orbital
quiz.why: The highest occupied orbital of N₂ is the bonding σ₂ₚ. Removing from it lowers the bond order from 3 to 2.5.

quiz.q: The six carbon p orbitals of benzene combine in MO theory to give
quiz.a: six π molecular orbitals, three bonding, holding six electrons
wrong: three π molecular orbitals, all bonding
six π molecular orbitals, all bonding
twelve π molecular orbitals, six of them bonding
quiz.why: N atomic orbitals always give N molecular orbitals, here half bonding and half antibonding. Six electrons fill the three bonding MOs, spread over the entire ring.

quiz.q: Which molecule can act as both a donor and an acceptor of hydrogen bonds?
quiz.why: Donation needs an H bonded to N, O or F, and acceptance needs a lone pair on one of those atoms. CH₃NH₂ has both. (CH₃)₃N and CH₃OCH₃ have lone pairs but no N–H or O–H, and CH₄ has neither.

quiz.q: What is the main attraction responsible for dissolving NaCl in water?
quiz.a: Ion–dipole forces between the ions and water molecules
wrong: Hydrogen bonds between Na⁺ and the hydrogen atoms of water
Dispersion forces between NaCl and water molecules
Dipole–dipole forces between NaCl units and water
quiz.why: An ion attracts the oppositely charged end of a polar water molecule. Ion–dipole forces are strong enough to offset the lattice energy of the salt.

quiz.q: Which compound should have the largest lattice energy?
wrong: All three are equal, because the ion charges are the same
quiz.why: With equal charges, lattice energy depends on the separation of the ions. F⁻ is the smallest anion, so NaF has the shortest distance and the strongest attraction.

quiz.q: Compared with an ion pair of charges +1 and −1, a pair of +3 and −3 ions at the same separation has a potential energy of attraction that is
quiz.why: Since E ∝ Q₁Q₂/r, tripling both charges multiplies the product by 3 × 3 = 9. This is why lattice energies rise steeply with ionic charge.

summary: Bond type follows electronegativity difference: ionic (large), polar covalent (intermediate), nonpolar covalent (zero). More shared pairs mean a shorter, stronger bond.
Lewis structures count valence electrons. Choose structures that minimize formal charge, and use resonance when several are equivalent. Know the octet-rule exceptions.
VSEPR counts electron domains to predict shape. Polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles.
Hybridization (sp, sp², sp³) describes σ frameworks. π bonds come from leftover p orbitals and prevent rotation.
MO theory fills bonding and antibonding orbitals. Bond order = ½(bonding − antibonding). It explains paramagnetic O₂ and delocalized π systems.
Dispersion, dipole–dipole and hydrogen-bonding forces determine physical properties. Metals have delocalized electrons. Lattice energy grows with charge and shrinks with size.

problems.q: Draw Lewis structures for ClF₃, CO₃²⁻ and NO₂⁻. Give the molecular geometry and the hybridization of the central atom in each.
problems.solution: ClF₃: 28 electrons. Cl has 3 bonds and 2 lone pairs: 5 domains, T-shaped, sp³d. CO₃²⁻: 24 electrons, three resonance structures, 3 domains: trigonal planar, sp². NO₂⁻: 18 electrons, two resonance structures with N having 2 bonded domains and 1 lone pair: bent (~115°), sp².
problems.a: ClF₃: T-shaped, sp³d. CO₃²⁻: trigonal planar, sp². NO₂⁻: bent, sp².

problems.q: Determine which are polar: SO₃, SO₂, PCl₃, PCl₅, ClF₃.
problems.solution: SO₃ is trigonal planar and symmetric: nonpolar. SO₂ is bent: polar. PCl₃ is pyramidal: polar. PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal and symmetric: nonpolar. ClF₃ is T-shaped: polar.
problems.a: Polar: SO₂, PCl₃, ClF₃. Nonpolar: SO₃, PCl₅.

problems.q: Write the MO configuration of CN⁻ and NO. Give each bond order and say whether it is paramagnetic.
problems.solution: CN⁻ has 10 valence electrons, isoelectronic with N₂: bond order 3, diamagnetic. NO has 11: the extra electron goes into π*₂ₚ, so bond order = (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5, with one unpaired electron: paramagnetic.
problems.a: CN⁻: bond order 3, diamagnetic. NO: bond order 2.5, paramagnetic.

problems.q: Explain why the boiling point of HF (19.5 °C) is much higher than that of HCl (−85 °C), though HCl has the larger mass.
problems.solution: F is small and highly electronegative, so the H–F bond is strongly polar, and HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds. HCl has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces. Hydrogen bonding outweighs the mass effect.

problems.q: Use lattice energies to explain why CaO (m.p. 2613 °C) melts much higher than KCl (m.p. 770 °C).
problems.solution: Lattice energy scales as Q₁Q₂/r. CaO has charges 2+ and 2−, so Q₁Q₂ = 4, against 1 for KCl. The ion separation is also smaller in CaO (100 + 140 = 240 pm against 138 + 181 = 319 pm for KCl). Both factors raise the lattice energy: about 5 times larger by the estimate 4 × 319/240, and 3401 against 715 kJ mol⁻¹ by experiment.
problems.a: CaO has a much larger lattice energy because of the 2+/2− charges.
